title: Ugali
subtitle: east african cornmeal staple
excerpt: A firm, smooth cornmeal porridge eaten daily across East Africa. It is cooked by stirring maize flour into boiling water until it pulls away from the sides of the pan.
sourceNotes: Ugali is the everyday staple of Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. It is traditionally made with white maize flour and served alongside meat, fish or vegetable stews.

recipe.batchNotes: Scale up in a larger pot. Stir more vigorously to prevent lumps in bigger quantities.

glossaryTerms.definition: East African cornmeal porridge cooked to a firm, smooth consistency and used to scoop stews.

content.text: is the daily staple for hundreds of millions of people across East Africa. It is made from just two ingredients: maize flour and water. The technique is simple but requires continuous stirring and confidence over heat to get a smooth, lump-free result.
White maize flour gives the most authentic result. Polenta is an acceptable substitute and widely available. The finished ugali should hold its shape when turned out onto a plate.
Bring the water to a full boil in a large saucepan over high heat.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the maize flour in a steady stream, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon. Work quickly to prevent lumps from forming.
Continue stirring vigorously for 5 minutes as the mixture thickens. It will become difficult to stir. That is correct.
Reduce the heat to low. Cover and cook for 10 minutes. Remove the lid and stir again from the base. The ugali should pull cleanly away from the sides of the pan.
Turn the ugali out onto a plate and shape into a smooth mound. Serve immediately alongside a stew or sauteed greens.
Add the flour more slowly next time and stir without stopping. If lumps form, press them against the side of the pan with the back of the spoon to break them down.

attrs.issue: Ugali is too soft to hold its shape

content.text: Cook for longer over low heat, stirring from the bottom every few minutes. If it is still soft, stir in another 30 g of maize flour mixed with a little cold water.

attrs.issue: Ugali is sticking and burning at the bottom

content.text: Lower the heat and stir more frequently. A heavy-based pan reduces hot spots. A small scorch at the very bottom is traditional and not a problem.

Ugali is eaten at least once a day by most Kenyan households. In Tanzania it is called ugali; in Uganda, posho. It is the food that holds the meal together. In Swahili culture, feeding someone ugali is an act of welcome. It has no flavour of its own but carries the flavour of everything served with it.
